title: MapReduce to Spark
description: Evolve from MapReduce word count to complex Spark joins, RDDs, lazy evaluation, DAG scheduler, Catalyst optimizer, Tungsten memory management, and shuffle optimization.

segments.text: MapReduce revolutionized batch processing at Google but has a fundamental limitation: every job writes intermediate results to disk. A multi-stage pipeline — filter, join, aggregate — means three rounds of disk I/O. Spark keeps data in memory between stages, running ten to one hundred times faster for iterative algorithms like PageRank and machine learning.

Resilient Distributed Datasets are Spark's core abstraction. An RDD is an immutable, partitioned collection distributed across a cluster. Transformations — map, filter, join — create new RDDs lazily. Actions — count, collect, save — trigger actual computation. This lazy evaluation lets Spark optimize the entire pipeline before executing anything.

Spark builds a DAG of stages from your transformations. Narrow transformations — map, filter — stay in the same stage. Wide transformations — groupBy, join — require a shuffle and create a new stage. The DAG scheduler determines stage boundaries and parallelism. More stages means more shuffles means slower execution — minimize wide transformations.

Spark SQL's Catalyst optimizer transforms logical query plans into optimized physical plans. It performs predicate pushdown — filter before join. Column pruning — read only needed columns. Join reordering — smallest table first. Catalyst uses rule-based and cost-based optimization, similar to traditional database optimizers but for distributed computation.

Your Spark job processes one terabyte of data with a large join. It's running for six hours and eventually fails with out-of-memory errors during the shuffle phase. What's happening and how do you fix it?
segments.thought_prompt: Diagnose a Spark job failing with OOM during shuffle on a 1TB join. Root cause and fix?

segments.text: Tungsten is Spark's memory management engine. Instead of JVM objects — which waste memory on headers and GC overhead — Tungsten stores data in raw binary format using sun.misc.Unsafe. This reduces memory usage by five to ten times and eliminates GC pauses. Cache-friendly data layouts improve CPU utilization by leveraging L1/L2 cache line locality.

Shuffle is Spark's most expensive operation. Data is repartitioned across the cluster — every executor sends data to every other executor. Shuffle optimization: use broadcast joins when one side is small enough to fit in memory — default under ten megabytes. Pre-partition data by join key. Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions from the default two hundred for large datasets.

Good partitioning is the key to Spark performance. Partition by the join key to enable co-located joins — no shuffle needed. Use repartition for full redistribution, coalesce to reduce partitions without shuffle. Aim for partition sizes between one hundred and two hundred megabytes. Too many small partitions create scheduling overhead, too few large ones create memory pressure.

Migrating from MapReduce to Spark: replace HDFS intermediate writes with in-memory caching. Replace multiple MR jobs with a single Spark DAG. Use DataFrames instead of raw RDDs for Catalyst optimization. LinkedIn's migration from MapReduce to Spark reduced ETL pipeline runtime from twelve hours to forty-five minutes.

Design a Spark pipeline that processes five terabytes of clickstream data daily: join with user profiles, compute per-user metrics, and output to a data warehouse. What partitioning, caching, and optimization strategies would you use?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a Spark pipeline for 5TB daily clickstream: joins, aggregations, partitioning strategy.

segments.text: Spark overcomes MapReduce's disk I/O bottleneck with in-memory computation, lazy evaluation with DAG optimization, Catalyst for query planning, Tungsten for memory efficiency, and intelligent shuffle management. The evolution from MapReduce to Spark mirrors the broader industry shift — most batch processing has moved to Spark or similar in-memory frameworks.
